text: To vitiate something is to spoil or weaken it so it no longer works properly. Here the Economist jokes that government baby-making campaigns are so cringe-inducing that they spoil the mood instead of exciting anyone.

A prophylactic is anything that prevents something unwelcome before it happens, such as a vaccine against disease. Here it is used loosely: gloomy books about parenthood protect readers from wanting children by putting them off in advance.
Precipitously means very steeply and suddenly, like dropping off a cliff. It comes from the same root as precipice. Here it describes a sharp fall in sperm counts in many countries.
To go to the dogs means to get worse or decline badly. The author uses it as a pun, since the story opens with pets replacing children in some countries.
In British English a buggy is a pushchair or stroller for a small child. Here the article means strollers for pets, which now outsell those for babies in South Korea.

Conceive has two meanings that the sentence plays on. To conceive of something is to imagine it, and to conceive is to become pregnant. The line says a puppy was once thought to make a couple imagine parenthood and then try for a baby.
A made-up word blending paw and paternity, the legal term for fatherhood. Pawternity leave is time off work to look after a new pet, copying paid parental leave.
Conventional wisdom is the view most people accept as true without checking it. The article says the old assumption, that a pet leads people toward children, is now being undermined.
To decry something is to publicly condemn it as bad. Here Pope Francis condemned the choice not to have children.
Frostily means in a cold, unfriendly way. The word fits the joke about a demographic winter, the pope's phrase for a population that is shrinking.
A phrase for a long period of falling birth rates and shrinking, ageing populations. Demography is the study of how populations change in size and makeup.

forms: biggest danger civilisation faces by far
text: This is a claim by Elon Musk, quoted to show how strongly some people feel about falling birth rates. Civilisation is the British spelling of civilization.
Gross domestic product, the total value of everything a country produces in a year. It is the most common measure of the size of an economy.
The average number of children per woman, about 2.1 in rich countries, at which each generation exactly replaces itself. Below it, a population eventually shrinks unless immigration fills the gap.
A deadly plague that swept Europe in the 1300s and killed tens of millions of people. The article uses it as the last time the world's population fell.
A Baroness is a woman who holds a title of nobility, here a seat in Britain's House of Lords. Lady is the polite way to address her, which is why the article switches between the two.
Camilla Cavendish's name for people who are delaying children or deciding against them. It plays on the way writers label generations, such as Generation Z.
An instinct is a natural urge that people feel without being taught. The quotation says the urge to continue the family line is fading.
If something is on the wane, it is growing weaker or less common, like the moon shrinking after it is full.
A sharp fall in the number of babies born. It is the opposite of a baby boom, such as the one in America after the Second World War.
Ageing is the British spelling of aging. An ageing society is one where the average person is getting older because fewer babies are born and people live longer.
To fuel growth means to supply the energy that makes an economy bigger. Young workers produce goods and services and pay taxes, so fewer of them means less growth.
Pensions are regular payments to people who have retired. In many countries today's workers pay for them through taxes.
Geopolitics is how geography, population and power shape the relations between countries. A country's size and the number of young people it has affect how strong it is.
Populous means having many people living there, so third-most-populous means third in the world by population. The article says Nigeria may overtake America for that spot by 2050.
If something is hotly debated, people argue about it with strong feelings. Here it warns that population forecasts decades ahead are uncertain.
To distract is to pull attention away from something else. The idea is that leaders might start a war abroad so voters stop focusing on problems at home.
Predominantly means mostly or mainly. Here it means that most of the people in a country follow one religion.
A drop in the number of relatives each person has. Kin means relatives, so fewer siblings means fewer cousins, aunts and uncles later.
Sombre is the British spelling of somber, meaning serious, dark and gloomy. The Beatles song about lonely people has a sad mood.
Baby fever is the strong wish to have a baby. Reverse baby fever is the author's joke for people who increasingly do not feel it.
Affordability is how easy it is for ordinary people to pay for something. Housing costs are a big part of why young adults hesitate to have children.
An adult who still lives in their parents' home. The article says it is hard to start a family while you feel like this.
The value of the best thing you give up when you choose something else. Raising a child takes so much time that the other things a person could do with it count as a cost.
An arms race is when rivals keep escalating to stay ahead. Here parents compete by paying for ever more lessons and tutoring so their children get into the best schools.
A style of raising children that demands a great deal of a parent's time, money and attention, such as constant lessons and supervision.
Helicopter parents hover over their children and manage everything; tiger parents push their children hard to achieve, especially in school. Both are labels for intensive parenting.
The way attitudes and behaviours spread from person to person like a cold, through friends, family and media. The author suggests wanting fewer children can spread this way.
To exalt something is to praise it highly. Here videos on TikTok present a life without children as wonderful.
A term for people who choose not to have children and see it as a positive. It is different from childless, which can suggest something is missing. The hashtag shows it is a social media trend.
A bucket list is a list of things you want to do before you die. Bucket-list travel means trips to famous places you have always wanted to see.
Dysfunctional means not working in a healthy way. A dysfunctional family has constant conflict or problems.
Telenovelas are Latin American television soap operas, with long dramatic stories. Brazilian ones are cited as evidence that TV can shape how many children people want.
A memoir is a book about the author's own life. Misery memoirs are books that complain about how hard parenthood and marriage can be.
To mirror something is to copy it exactly, like a reflection. The Polish women's family size comes to match that of their new country.
Searing means intensely critical, like a burning heat. The author is harshly critical of fertility clinics.
In vitro fertilisation: doctors combine an egg and sperm in a laboratory dish and then place the resulting embryo in the womb. It helps some people who cannot conceive naturally.
A medical process that freezes a woman's eggs so she may try to have a baby later. It is not guaranteed to work.
Rosier means more hopeful or optimistic, from the saying about seeing things through rose-coloured glasses. The clinics paint a better picture than the data support.
A joke word mixing sperm and apocalypse, meaning a disaster that ends everything. It refers to the steep fall in sperm counts.
The idea that there is a limited window of years in which a person can easily have a child, so time is running out. It is a metaphor, not a real clock.
To baby-proof a house is to make it safe for a small child. The author twists it to ask how to protect society from the baby bust.
To titillate is to excite or arouse someone, often in a mild way. It rhymes with vitiate, which the author chose on purpose for the joke.
Something cringe-inducing is so awkward or embarrassing that it makes you wince. The Danish adverts and Singapore rap are the examples.
Conception is when a pregnancy begins. The Danish advert joked that couples on holiday should send proof in order to win prizes.
A civic duty is something a citizen should do for the good of the country, such as voting or serving on a jury. The rap jokes about making babies this way.
A brainteaser is a puzzle that makes you think hard. Here it means an idea that is not simple to judge.
A proxy is someone allowed to act for another person. A proxy vote is a vote cast on behalf of someone else, here a parent voting for a child.
A demographer is a scientist who studies populations: how many people there are, their ages and how those numbers change.
A mantle is a cloak, and in politics it stands for a duty or role someone takes on. Here the author doubts any politician would take up this idea.
Self-interest is care for your own benefit. Older voters tend to want more spending on health care, which helps them, than on schools.
